Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Etruscan Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Etruscan script is a similar script to Latin, derived from Greek.
Knowledge.Name: Etruscan Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Aramaic Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Aramaic script is a form of Phoenician designed, an Abjad, which is used extensively in the Levantine to write various triconsonantal languages.
Knowledge.Name: Aramaic Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Syriac Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Syriac script is a cursive form of Aramaic designed to write the dialect of the Syriac people, but which is widely applied to other languages of the Fertile Crescent.
Knowledge.Name: Syriac Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Nabatean Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Nabatean script is an abjad based on Aramaic that is used in the Kingdom of Nabatea to write their dialect of Arabic.
Knowledge.Name: Nabatean Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Phoenician Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Phoenician script is an abjad originally based on modified Egyptian hieroglyphs that influenced almost all of the writing systems in Europe, Asia and Africa. It is designed to write triconsonantal languages and therefore does not contain vowels. In Hebrew, this script is usually called "Old Hebrew" and in Aramaic it is known as "Samaritan".
Knowledge.Name: Phoenician Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Ashurit Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Ashurit script is an abjad used to write the Hebrew language, sometimes also known as Hebrew Square script.
Knowledge.Name: Ashurit Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Coptic Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Coptic script is derived from the Greek script and is used to write the Coptic language in Egypt.
Knowledge.Name: Coptic Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Tartesian Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: This script, related to Phoenician, was used to write the Tartessian language prior to the Romanization of this area.
Knowledge.Name: Tartesian Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Meridional Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: This script, related to Phoenician and possibly Ionic Greek was used to write the Iberian language prior to the Romanization of this area.
Knowledge.Name: Meridional Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Levantine Iberian Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Levantine Iberian script, also known as the Northern Iberian script, was used to write both the Iberian and Celtiberian languages prior to the Romanisation of this area.
Knowledge.Name: Levantine Iberian Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Greco-Iberian Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Greco-Iberian script was a script adapted from a subset of Ionic Greek with several additions that was used to write the Iberian language, in addition to its other native scripts.
Knowledge.Name: Greco-Iberian Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Neo-Assyrian Cuneiform Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: Neo-Assyrian Cuneiform was originally designed to write the Akkadian language but largely survives in educated circles in Parthia, where it is used to write Parthian.
Knowledge.Name: Neo-Assyrian Cuneiform Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Persian Cuneiform Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: Persian Cuneiform is an archaic way of writing the Ariyan language (also known as Old Persian).
Knowledge.Name: Persian Cuneiform Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Egyptian Hieroglyhpic Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: Egyptian Hieroglyphs are an archaic writing form still seen in monumental form in Egypt. It is a largely logographic system but it does have some phoenetic elements.
Knowledge.Name: Egyptian Hieroglyhpic Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Hieratic Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: Hieratic is an archaic curvsive written form of Egyptian Hieroglyphs used by scholars in the late classical period.
Knowledge.Name: Hieratic Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Demotic Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: Demotic is an semi-archaic evolution of the earlier Hieratic script, which primarily survives in formal writing and scribes writing both the Demotic and Coptic languages.
Knowledge.Name: Demotic Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Meroitic Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Meroitic alphasyllabary was used in the Kingdom of Kush in hieroglyphic and cursive forms.
Knowledge.Name: Meroitic Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Latin Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Latin script is the script that the Romans use to write the Latin language. It is derived from the closely related Etruscan script. It is also often applied to the languages of subjects and neighbours as they Latinize.
Knowledge.Name: Latin Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Greek Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: Greek letters were also used to record foreign names and short texts around the Black Sea.
Knowledge.Name: Greek Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Phrygian Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Phrygian script is an alphabetic script used for the language of the same name using Greek-looking symbols but with often different values for the sounds.
Knowledge.Name: Phrygian Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Lydian Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Lydian script is an alphabetic script used for the language of the same name using Greek-looking symbols but with often different values for the sounds.
Knowledge.Name: Lydian Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Carian Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Carian script is an alphabetic script used for the Anatolian dialect of the same name.
Knowledge.Name: Carian Script

Knowledge.Description: Knowledge of the use of the Sidetic Script
Knowledge.LongDescription: The Sidetic script is an alphabetic script used for the language of the same name using Greek-looking symbols but with often different values for the sounds.
Knowledge.Name: Sidetic Script

<Definition>
  <NameEntryRegex><![CDATA[^(?:(?<adultname>[\w'-]+) )(?<ownername>[^ "]+)(?: \"(?<birthname>[\w '-]+)\")$]]></NameEntryRegex>
  <Elements>
    <Element Name="Real Name" Usage="0" MinimumCount="1" MaximumCount="1"><![CDATA[Whether you were born a slave or whether you became a slave later in life, you will nonetheless have been given a name by your parents. This is your real name, probably one of the few connections you have to anything outside of your current circumstances.

You may or may not tell other people this name, but even if it is known, it would only be used now in the most private of settings.]]></Element>
    <Element Name="Slave Name" Usage="4" MinimumCount="1" MaximumCount="1"><![CDATA[Your slave name is the name that your owner has given to you. This is the name that you will most often be addressed by amongst the company of other slaves working for your master, and potentially by your master and their family as well.

It could be as simple as a name like Servus or Serva (meaning slave), but the Romans also love to name their slaves after historical or contemporary figures. You may find yourself a Hannibal, Romulus, Cato, or Cleopatra.

In some cases, your slave name could also be the same as your real name, particularly if you were either Greek or well-known before becoming a slave.]]></Element>
    <Element Name="Owner Name" Usage="14" MinimumCount="1" MaximumCount="1"><![CDATA[Your owner name is a name derived from your owner's Praenomen. This is the name that others from outside your master's household will call you, and is common to all slaves of the same gender in the household. Your master may call you by this name when addressing you, but when talking about you will probably use your slave name.

If you are a male, it will be the owner's praenomen with the suffix -por. Examples include Cassipor (from Cassius), Marcipor (from Marcus), Gaipor (from Gaius), etc.

If you are a female, it will be the owner's wife's praenomen with the suffix -ae, for example Liviae (from Livia), Juliae (from Julia), Maximae (from Maxima), etc.]]></Element>
  </Elements>
  <Patterns>
    <Pattern Style="3" Params="0" Text="{0}" />
    <Pattern Style="2" Params="4,14" Text="{0} {1}" />
    <Pattern Style="5" Params="4,14" Text="{0} {1}" />
    <Pattern Style="1" Params="4" Text="{0}" />
    <Pattern Style="0" Params="4" Text="{0}" />
    <Pattern Style="4" Params="14" Text="{0}" />
  </Patterns>
</Definition>

<Definition>
  <NameEntryRegex><![CDATA[^(?:(?<birthname>[\w'-]+))\s+(?<matronym>[\w'-]+)\s*(?<patronym>[\w'-]+)*$]]></NameEntryRegex>
  <Elements>
    <Element Name="Given Name" Usage="0" MinimumCount="1" MaximumCount="1"><![CDATA[Your given name is a name given to you by your mother eight days after you are born. Your given name is usually unique amongst your sisters, but deceased older siblings' names are often reused.

The Gauls have a long history of contact with both Greek and Latin speaking peoples, and some of their names are influenced by or corrupted forms of names from Hellenistic or Latin sources.

You can use the following generator if you are unsure: https://www.fantasynamegenerators.com/celtic-gaul-names.php
#1Note: names that end in "o" or "u" in this generator should be read as ending in "on" and "a" respectively#0]]></Element>
    <Element Name="Matronym" Usage="8" MinimumCount="1" MaximumCount="1"><![CDATA[Your matronym derives from your mother, and is simply a modified version of her name. It is used primarily prior to marriage, after which it is more common to use your husband's patronym instead.

In Gaulish names, the matronym is formed by taking the genitive case of the mother's given name. A simplified version of these rules is as follows:

1) If the mother's name ends in #6a#0, add an #6s#0 (e.g. #BVerica#0 -> #BVericas#0)
2) If the mother's name ends in #6us/os#0, drop the #6us#0 or #6os#0 and add #6i#0 (e.g. #BMattus#0 -> #BMatti#0)
3) If the mother's name ends in #6is#0, drop the #6is#0 and add #6eis#0 (e.g. #BVocagnis#0 -> #BVocagneis#0)]]></Element>
    <Element Name="Patronym" Usage="7" MinimumCount="0" MaximumCount="1"><![CDATA[Your patronym is a modified version of your husband's given name, and is adopted as your primary surname after you are married. If you are unmarried, you should not select one.

In Gaulish names, the patronym is formed by taking the genitive case of your husband's given name. A simplified version of these rules is as follows:

1) If the husband's name ends in #6ir#0, drop the #6ir#0 and add an #6ros#0 (e.g. #BDattovir#0 -> #BDattovros#0)
2) If the husband's name ends in #6us/os#0, drop the #6us#0 or #6os#0 and add #6i#0 (e.g. #BAlpus#0 -> #BAlpi#0)
3) If the husband's name ends in #6is#0, drop the #6is#0 and add #6eis#0 (e.g. #BLitavis#0 -> #BLitaveis#0)
4) If the husband's name otherwise ends in a consonant, simply add #6i#0 (e.g. #BCaticorix#0 -> #BCaticorixi#0)]]></Element>
  </Elements>
  <Patterns>
    <Pattern Style="3" Params="0" Text="{0}" />
    <Pattern Style="2" Params="0,7,8" Text="{0} ?1[{1}][{2}]" />
    <Pattern Style="5" Params="0,7,8" Text="{0} ?1[{1} nata {2}][{2}]" />
    <Pattern Style="1" Params="0,7,8" Text="{0} ?1[{1}][{2}]" />
    <Pattern Style="0" Params="0" Text="{0}" />
    <Pattern Style="4" Params="7,8" Text="?0[{0}][{1}]" />
  </Patterns>
</Definition>
